name: Priya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential. Can you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a crew foreperson at Kessel Valley Power, the public electricity company for our valley, and I run a crew of four. We're at the depot by six, I go over the job sheets with Kofi, our planner, and then we're out replacing old poles, stringing new line or chasing faults. My favourite part is the climb itself, being up there with the whole valley under you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay, and the nights. We're on the public pay scale, which is lower than what the private contractors get, and the storm overtime is what actually pays the rent on our flat. My partner Dev works nights at a care home, so some weeks we only see each other in the car park.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, and ask a few questions about each.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go ahead. I should say I don't use any of the AI stuff, so you're getting someone who only knows it from the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the lines don't care about hype. Somebody still has to climb a forty-foot pole in sleet and swap a blown transformer. I'd probably post something like that on the union group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays about as tight as it is now. Rent on our flat went up again in spring, Dev's care home hours are all over the place, and I've got maybe three weeks of money in the bank. AI not changing much doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do: run my crew and take every storm callout I can get. At the next union meeting I'd push again to close the pay gap with the private contractors, and I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which I promise myself every January. And I'd fight any new app management tries to put on our trucks, because saving time usually means cutting a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat. Relieved that the work's safe, tired that the money never gets easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said saving time usually means cutting a person. Where have you seen that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago they brought in a scheduling system and used the hours it saved to stop replacing a lineman who retired. My crew went from five to four, and nobody called it a cut. So even when the tech is boring, I watch what they do with the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight one month, which bill would go unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck payment, because the dealer gives you a grace month and the landlord doesn't. Dev and I have done that dance twice already. It's not a crisis, it's just how the month goes on the public utility's pay scale.

say: The **power lines** don't care about hype; someone still climbs the pole in sleet.
I'd post on the **union group chat** that our work is safe and leave it there.
think: My life stays as **tight** as it is now, with rent up again in spring.
With about **three weeks** of money saved, AI not changing much fixes nothing.
do: Take every **storm callout** I can get and run my crew as normal.
Push the union to close the **pay gap** with private contractors.
Fight any **new app** on the trucks, because saved time usually means a cut person.
feel: **Relieved** that the work is safe, but **tired** that money never gets easier.
S0.quote: My crew went from five to four, and nobody called it a cut.
fieldNote: Her distrust of tech comes from a **scheduling system** that quietly cost her crew a lineman.
Money stress is **already here**: rising rent and a truck payment she sometimes skips.
She sees everything through the **union** and the pay gap with private contractors.

steps.text: Take every storm callout through the winter
Raise the contractor pay gap at the next union meeting
Put fifty a month into savings from January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stand with the people in the call centre and the design office, because they go first. Our union local covers them too, and I've known Rosa on the outage phones since my first year. I'd say it loud at work: if the company saves money on software, it can pay the crews properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it comes for my overtime before it comes for my job. If the software gets good at predicting where lines will fail and planning the work, there are fewer midnight callouts, and those callouts are how we make rent. A smart planner saving the company overtime is a pay cut for me with a nice name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my name on the union's technology committee in the first month, even though I hate meetings, so somebody who actually climbs is in the room. I'd ask for weekend shifts on the tree-trimming contract to make up the overtime. I won't learn the new systems for fun; I'll learn what I'm forced to and not a button more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I'm good at the job, and it still feels like the ground under the job is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa on the outage phones first, because answering customers is right there on the list you read out. Then Kofi, our planner, who's fifty-eight and still does the job sheets by hand. Those two have kept my crew safe for years, and I don't know what I'd say to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only learn what you're forced to. Doesn't that put you at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've watched people chase every new tool and get nothing for it but more work. I'd rather be the person who knows the lines blind than the one who knows the app, and learning to love software at this point isn't me. If that's a risk, it's one I'm choosing.

say: Stand with the **call centre** and design office staff, because their work goes first.
If the company saves on **software**, it can afford to pay the crews properly.
think: The software comes for my **overtime** before it comes for my job.
Fewer **midnight callouts** means less rent money, whatever the company calls it.
do: Join the union's **technology committee** in the first month so a climber is in the room.
Ask for **weekend shifts** on the tree-trimming contract to cover lost overtime.
Learn only the **required systems**, and not a button more.
feel: **Anxious**, because being good at the job no longer feels like enough.
S1.quote: A smart planner saving the company overtime is a pay cut for me with a nice name.
fieldNote: She reads the threat as lost **overtime**, not lost work, which is a sharp reading.
Her worry for older office colleagues shows real **loyalty** across the union.
She openly **chooses** not to learn new tools and owns that risk.

steps.text: Sign up for the union's technology committee in the first month
Take weekend shifts on the tree-trimming contract
Keep climbing and running her crew without extra training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why the grid should stay publicly owned, so the gains don't vanish into some tech firm. I'd be at every rally and I'd say it on the union chat until people muted me. Lights are a public thing, and the robots should be too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think I've got about five years of climbing left and then nothing. By 2028 a machine plans my jobs, writes the switching orders and tells my crew where to stand. By 2031 a robot is up the pole, and I'm thirty-two with no savings in a valley with one power company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Dev and I would stop talking about a bigger flat and sign another year where we are. I'd put every overtime payment in a separate account, even if it's only a few hundred. I'd push the union to bargain for a guaranteed job or a payout for every lineworker the robots replace, and I'd vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like watching a storm front on the radar that's headed straight for your house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years for the thinking side, about five for the climbing. What do those three years in between look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be the strangest years of my life. I'd still be up the poles, taking orders from a screen, and knowing the screen is training the thing that replaces me. I'd work every shift I could in those years, because that's the last real money I'd see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we were right never to buy a house, which is a sad thing to be right about. Then I'd say we need to think about where people still need hands, maybe care work like Dev does. And I'd probably cry in the truck the next morning, where nobody sees.

say: This is why the **grid** should stay publicly owned, so the gains stay public.
I'd be at every **rally** and on the union chat until people muted me.
think: I have about **five years** of climbing left, then nothing in this valley.
By 2028 a machine **plans** my jobs; by 2031 a **robot** climbs the pole.
do: Sign another year on the **current flat** instead of moving somewhere bigger.
Put every **overtime** payment into a separate account, however small.
Push the union to win a **guaranteed job or payout** for replaced lineworkers.
feel: **Alarmed**, like watching a storm front on radar heading straight for home.
I'd **cry in the truck** the next morning, where nobody sees.
S2.quote: I'd still be up the poles, taking orders from a screen, and knowing the screen is training the thing that replaces me.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** as her last real earning window and would work it hard.
Her answer is **collective**: public ownership, union bargaining and voting for a guarantee.
Thinking about **care work** like her partner's was the first sign of her bending.

steps.text: Renew the lease on the current flat for one more year
Move every overtime payment into a separate savings account
Push the union to bargain for a job or payout guarantee
Vote for candidates promising support for replaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, but with a calmer face: we have five years, so let's use them to write the rules. Who's responsible when a robot drops a live wire? Who checks its work? I'd want lineworkers writing those answers, not a sales team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me time to be angry and then do something, which two years doesn't. The planning side of my job goes in 2031 and the climbing around 2034, so I'd be thirty-five. That's young enough to start again, but I'd be starting with nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run for the union's full-time safety rep job at the next election, because someone has to sign off that the machines are safe near people. I'd try to save properly, maybe two hundred a month, by selling my truck and sharing Dev's car. And I'd keep climbing every shift until the day they tell me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of air in it. I can see the wall, but I can also see myself walking toward it with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell your truck. How big a step is that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big. That truck is the first thing I ever bought with line money, and I'm still paying it off. Selling it means admitting this is real, and I hate admitting things are real before they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a safety rep and not something completely new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know where people get hurt, and robots won't change that for a while. If machines are working next to live lines and next to people, someone who's been burned on a pole should be checking them. Learning to code at thirty-five isn't me, but checking a robot's work is.

say: Five years is enough time for lineworkers to **write the rules** for robots.
Someone must decide who is **responsible** when a robot drops a live wire.
think: Five years gives me time to be **angry** and then act, unlike two.
I'd be **thirty-five** when the climbing goes, young enough but starting with nothing.
do: Run for the union's full-time **safety rep** job at the next election.
Sell the **truck** and share my partner's car to save two hundred a month.
Keep **climbing** every shift until the company tells me to stop.
feel: **Anxious**, but with some air in it, because there's room for a plan.
S3.quote: Learning to code at thirty-five isn't me, but checking a robot's work is.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn her from **despair** into a concrete union plan.
Selling the **truck** felt bigger to her than any career move.
She picks **safety checking** over coding because it uses what she already knows.

steps.text: Run for the union's full-time safety representative job
Sell the pickup and share her partner's car
Save two hundred a month once the truck is gone
Keep climbing every shift until told to stop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if the government wastes it, that's on them. Companies buying the robots could pay right now to train every lineworker for whatever comes next. I'd say that at work and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is long enough that I might just pretend it isn't happening for the first five. I know that's not smart. But the next eight or nine years look like my normal job, and I'd be nearly forty when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the safety inspector certificate over two winters, at night, because the union pays half the fee. Dev and I would still plan to have a kid in a few years, but we'd want one of us in a job that isn't on a robot list. And I'd keep pushing the union, because ten years is about how long a good contract fight takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Most days I'd forget about it, and then a robot video would come up and ruin my lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might pretend it isn't happening. What would snap you out of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the first time the company tests a climbing robot on our lines and asks my crew to babysit it. Watching a machine on our own poles would make it real in a way the news never does. I'd sign up for the inspector course that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this change your plans for a child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me want the child more, oddly, and want a steadier floor under it. I grew up with a dad who lost his mill job when I was nine, and I remember the quiet in the house. I don't want my kid to remember that kind of quiet.

say: **Ten years** is a gift, and if the government wastes it, that's on them.
Companies buying **robots** should pay to train the people they replace.
think: I might **pretend** it isn't happening for the first five years.
The next nine years look like my **normal job**, and I'd be nearly forty after.
do: Study for the **safety inspector** certificate over two winters, half paid by the union.
Keep **pushing the union**, because a good contract fight takes about ten years.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly forgotten until a robot video ruins my lunch.
S4.quote: I grew up with a dad who lost his mill job when I was nine, and I remember the quiet in the house.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her honest about **denial**, and she names what would end it.
Her father's lost **mill job** shapes how she thinks about having a child.
She still plans a **child**, but wants one parent in a robot-proof job.

steps.text: Take the safety inspector certificate at night over two winters
Press the union for a retraining fund paid by employers
Plan a child with her partner once one job is steadier

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without question, because there's no time to save and no other power company in the valley to go to. What would help is a written promise. If a robot takes a lineworker's job, that person gets paid retraining or a real payout, by law. Not a leaflet, a law.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. If Kessel Valley Power owns them and stays public, the savings could go to cheaper bills and decent pensions. If some private firm owns them, the valley pays more for less, and we're the ones out of work.

headlineQuote: If a robot takes a lineworker's job, that person gets paid retraining or a real payout, by law. Not a leaflet, a law.
portrait: Priya Silva, 27, runs a **four-person crew** at a public power company in a river valley.
She lives on **thin savings** with her partner, and storm overtime pays the rent.
She avoids new tech after a **scheduling system** quietly cost her crew a lineman.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** to **alarmed** at AGI in two years, easing with more time.
Every answer runs through the **union**, public ownership and a legal promise for replaced workers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to save and no other power company nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** guaranteeing paid retraining or a real payout to any lineworker a robot replaces.
Keeping the **robots publicly owned**, so the savings go to cheaper bills and pensions.
